what_it_does: AI accelerator chips are essentially big grids of tiny multiply-and-add units (called MACs — Multiply-Accumulate units) that do the core math of neural networks; researchers usually optimize how data flows across the grid, but rarely look inside each individual MAC unit to see if the bit-level arithmetic can be improved. This paper introduces a new way of thinking about those MAC units by treating the 'bit weight' — how many bits represent each number — as an extra dimension to optimize across, alongside the existing spatial and temporal dimensions. From this viewpoint the authors derive four concrete design transformations that reduce timing delay, chip area, or power consumption within the MAC itself. They apply these ideas across four established grid architectures (including a grid where data ripples through like a wave, called a systolic array) using a 28-nanometer chip design process. This is based on the abstract; exact improvement numbers are not confirmed.
